title: Short Stuff: Wigs in English Court
summary: Short Stuff episode explaining why barristers and judges in Britain wear powdered wigs in court. The hosts distinguish barristers from solicitors, describe the wigs' purposes (formality, solemnity, anonymity in criminal court), their origin in the 1600s, and their link to syphilis-related hair loss and Louis XIV's fashion influence. They cover wig styles (judges' fuller, longer wigs versus barristers' smaller ones), cost and horsehair construction, the decline of wig fashion, and the 2007 and 2011 changes that ended wig use in civil courts and for judges, with wigs still used in criminal cases. They note former British colonies dropping wigs and that Hong Kong still uses them.

segments.title: Opening banter on court wigs
segments.summary: Hosts joke about modern photos of barristers and judges in powdered wigs and introduce the question of why lawyers wear them in Britain.

segments.title: Barrister vs solicitor
segments.summary: Josh explains that solicitors advise clients outside court, while barristers represent clients in court and petition the court on their behalf; barristers wear wigs and solicitors do not.

segments.title: Purposes of wigs and origins in court
segments.summary: The wigs are called periwigs and were meant to give proceedings a formal, solemn air and to provide a sort of anonymity in criminal court. British courts adopted them around 1685 after earlier portraits showed none.

segments.title: Wig styles, cost and horsehair
segments.summary: Barristers' wigs are smaller with curled sides and back; judges' wigs are fuller and longer, which distinguishes them. Judges may spend about three thousand dollars and barristers five hundred to a thousand. Wigs are traditionally made of horsehair, though goat hair, cotton, and historically donated human hair have also been used.

segments.title: Syphilis, Louis XIV and the fashion of wigs
segments.summary: Hair loss from syphilis, plus long hair being fashionable, helped drive wig use. Louis XIV, who reigned 1643 to 1715, popularized powdered wigs across European courts, including England under Charles the Second. Wig fashion faded in less than a century.

segments.title: Decline of wigs and modern reforms
segments.summary: Wigs remained for coachmen, bishops and the court after fashion moved on; bishops stopped in the 1830s. A 2007 court challenge ended barrister wigs in civil court, and judges stopped in 2011, while criminal cases still use them. Former British colonies such as Jamaica and Australia dropped wigs, and Hong Kong still uses them.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts joke about visiting Hong Kong to see wigs and sign off with an email address for listener contact.
